US debt hits $40 trillion: Who does Washington owe and why does it matter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
13:18:31 UTC
22:18:31 KST

US debt hits $40 trillion: Who does Washington owe and why does it matter?
Heavy borrowing, increased spending and tax cuts by Democratic and Republican administrations have long raised concern.
The total debt of the United States has surpassed $40 trillion for the first time in history, according to a Department of the Treasury update on Wednesday.
Ballooning debt, especially during President Donald Trump’s second term, which began in January last year, has been raising concerns about a looming fiscal crisis for some time, with economists fearing a toxic combination of heavy borrowing, increased spending and lower taxes could land the world’s biggest economy in crisis.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4CEO pay skyrockets in 2025 amid growing income inequality in the US
- list 2 of 4Inside the UK’s ‘stressful’ cost of living crisis Burnham hopes to tackle
- list 3 of 4UAE trade embargo could shut Iran’s key economic escape route: Here’s why
- list 4 of 4US national debt passes record $40 trillion
Fast-rising US debt comes despite Trump’s championing of cost-cutting and efficiency as a hallmark of his second term, with the nongovernmental Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) slashing between 250,000 and 350,000 federal jobs and cutting global aid since the start of last year.
In May 2023, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) predicted that the US would reach the $40 trillion mark in 2028.
Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB), a budget watchdog, said in a statement, “$40 trillion of debt doesn’t exist solely on the government’s ledgers; it is felt throughout the economy and finds its way to the pocketbooks of people one way or another.”
Here’s what we know about why US debt is rising, and why it matters:
How fast is debt rising?
US debt is growing much faster in the 2020s than it did in previous decades.
Total debt, which includes debt owed to others and what the government owes itself, has doubled since January 2017, when Trump began his first term as president. US debt at the time was $19.95 trillion.
During Trump’s first term, public debt rose by $7.8 trillion, most of it because of the cost of the COVID-19 pandemic response. Since his return to office in January 2025, debt has grown by $3.8 trillion, amounting to a total of $11.6 trillion across his two terms so far.
Under the Biden administration from 2021 to 2025, the government continued to borrow and spend heavily in response to the pandemic; debt rose by $8.4 trillion.
US debt hit $39 trillion in March this year, meaning it took fewer than five months to pile on an additional $1 trillion in debt.
For comparison, it took close to 200 years for total US debt to cross $1 trillion for the first time in 1981, according to analysis by CRFB, although $1 trillion in 1981 would be worth $3.67 trillion in real terms today, after inflation is taken into account.
The CBO estimates that debt will rise from 101 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026 to 120 percent in 2036. That is well above the previous US record of 106 percent after World War II.
Why is debt ballooning?
Crisis spending
There have been two major crises in nearly two decades, during which governments have needed to borrow and increase spending.
The 2007-09 recession was the first crisis, while the second was the 2020-23 COVID-19 pandemic, which is linked to about one-third of the debt run up since 2017, as borrowing under both the Trump and Joe Biden presidencies intensified.
Tax revenue too low
Analysts say another reason for rising borrowing is that tax and other revenues are not keeping up with spending, especially as the US is spending more to fund pensions and healthcare for an ageing population.
Experts say Democratic and Republican administrations alike have failed to rein in spending or raise taxes to close this gap.
The US spends about $7 trillion annually, with about 60 percent of that going to Social Security Administration (SSA) payments, health insurance including Medicare and Medicaid, and veterans’ care.
Revenues are inadequate to meet these expenses. For example, in July, the US brought in $334bn in individual income taxes, social insurance, corporate taxes and others, according to the Treasury Department.
However, it paid out $766bn, almost double the revenue, in social security, health insurance, national defence and interest payments.
Rising interest rates
Interest rates remained low until the pandemic hit, at which point the Federal Reserve raised rates to fight inflation.
Now, the US is paying about $1.1 trillion annually to service its debt, slightly more than it spends on defence. In the first 10 months of the 2026 budget year, interest costs have also eclipsed health insurance spending and are now the second-largest slice of spending after pensions. It spends between $1.8 trillion and $2 trillion per year on federal retirement benefits – Social Security – and state or local public pensions combined, according to data from analysis group USA Facts.
What tax cuts has Trump introduced
Despite these rising costs, Trump has implemented deep tax cuts for businesses, starting with his Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 during his first term, which slashed the corporate tax rate from 35 percent to 21 percent.
He followed that up in 2025 with his “One Beautiful Bill Act”, permanently entrenching the 2017 law. Although the bill also cut Medicaid spending by 12 percent, it raised the debt ceiling by nearly $5 trillion to allow for this.
At present, individual income taxes make up roughly half of federal revenues, compared with only 9 percent from corporate income taxes.
In between the two Trump presidencies, the Biden administration also spent heavily on infrastructure investment and clean energy subsidies.
Who is the US in debt to?
Public debt borrowed from domestic and foreign investors makes up 80 percent – roughly $32 trillion – of the gross debt, according to Treasury data.
About $21 trillion of this public debt is owed domestically, to a variety of creditors including the Federal Reserve ($4.528 trillion), which buys and sells Treasury securities to influence federal interest rates and manage the money supply, according to analysis by the Peter G Peterson Foundation.
Other creditors are mutual funds ($5.195 trillion), pension funds ($1.135 trillion), state and local governments ($1.636 trillion), commercial banks and depository Institutions ($2.083 trillion) and other corporate and individual lenders ($6.660 trillion).
Internationally, the US is in debt to several countries and private investors. In 1970, total foreign debt holders accounted for 5 percent of gross debt, but by 2025, they made up 32 percent. That means while they are helping boost US economic activity, more of the country’s income is being sent abroad in the form of interest payments.
By 2025, the US owed Japan $1.203 trillion, the United Kingdom ($889bn), China ($683bn), as well as more than 30 other entities.
Separately, another 20 percent of the gross national debt – about $8 trillion – is owed intra-governmentally and therefore does not affect overall finances.
What does rising debt mean for the US economy?
Analysts say the rising debt could potentially create an economic crisis for the US, in the form of hyperinflation or higher interest rates, for example, if it goes unchecked.
As more debt piles on, there is a growing risk that private investment will fall because of safety concerns, and as a consequence, economic growth could slow down.
Lawmakers may eventually be forced to respond with painful austerity measures such as higher taxes, analysts say. Social safety net programmes could also be at risk.
It could take years to resolve, experts warn, and the consequences could be intergenerational, with young people forced to pay more for many years.
The rest of the world would be affected too: the US is a cornerstone of the global economy, and a crisis there will likely hurt global markets.
The first correcting step, MacGuineas of CRFB said, is to commit to zero new borrowing immediately. Lawmakers must also set up a bipartisan fiscal commission to scrutinise the issues, she said. With a commitment to keep taxes low and reduce spending, while also engaging in a hugely expensive war in the Middle East, this may be difficult to achieve, analysts say.

1 month in office: UK’s Burnham faces growing economic test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
13:17:38 UTC
22:17:38 KST

- Experts say tackling the cost of living, reviving weak growth, and restoring the UK's strained public finances remain Burnham's top challenges
- The biggest challenge is the economy – how to get sustainable growth – and the public finances – how to bring down public debt without sacrificing social priorities,' Patrick Diamond, professor of public policy at Queen Mary University of London, tells Anadolu
-  Politically, Burnham must work quickly to restore trust and deliver visible, short‑term improvements while sequencing longer‑term industrial and skills investments,' says Amelia Hadfield, head of politics department at University of Surrey
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces serious economic challenges a month into his premiership, with experts warning that tackling the cost of living, reviving weak growth, and restoring the country’s strained public finances will be key to delivering on his domestic agenda.
It has been a month since Burnham officially became prime minister on July 17, with his pledges focusing on cost-of-living relief, devolving power from Westminster, and bringing essential services under public control.
However, experts have warned that obstacles such as post-Brexit economic challenges, as well as the complex domestic agenda he inherited, could make it difficult for him to deliver on his goals.
In an interview with Anadolu, Patrick Diamond, professor of public policy at Queen Mary University of London, said that bringing down the cost of living by cutting energy bills and the price of public transport is the pressing factor for Burnham.
"The biggest challenge is the economy – how to get sustainable growth – and the public finances – how to bring down public debt without sacrificing social priorities," he noted.
Reiterating the economy as the biggest obstacle for the new premier, Diamond underlined that post-Brexit, the UK economy is weak and there has been a marked deterioration in the UK’s fiscal position.
He went on to say that the economy is not growing above 1.5%, which is "not enough to support the welfare state and public services."
"Any government in Britain is constrained in what it can do due to that underlying economic weakness," he added.
For Diamond, the cost of living is a good place to start for Burnham as an immediate priority to build public confidence.
However, he said the government has to show that it can also improve competitiveness and make the private sector economy work more efficiently by reducing red tape, and making it easier to start and grow a business.
"It is not enough to redistribute the cake more fairly – it is essential to also make the cake bigger," said Diamond. 
'Burnham must work quickly to restore trust'
Amelia Hadfield, head of the politics department at the University of Surrey, said that Burnham inherits a "complex, compound domestic agenda," from persistent regional inequality to stalled productivity that demand tangible place‑based wins.
For her, acute cost‑of‑living pressures and public service backlogs such as health, social care, and housing could undermine public confidence, which could make things more difficult for Burnham.
She also stressed energy security and the need to accelerate clean electrification while protecting industry are also among challenges for Burnham.
"Politically, Burnham must work quickly to restore trust and deliver visible, short‑term improvements while sequencing longer‑term industrial and skills investments," Hadfield noted.
She went on to say that Burnham will need to "balance urgency with the institutional reform" needed to sustain them.
Hadfield suggested that devolution and "place-based" initiatives, skills and employment, and kickstarting infrastructure acceleration by committing streamlined planning windows should be prioritized by the new government during the first 100 days.
However, she warned that the current situation of public finance and economic pressure may affect the prime minister's plans.
"Burnham’s delivery goals may likely collide with constrained public finances and competing fiscal pressures, limiting the speed and scale of place deals," she added.
Hadfield noted that "Whitehall fragmentation" and "historically siloed departmental incentives" and slow procurement/legal processes will impede rapid rollout.
She underlined that powerful sectoral lobbies and incumbent interests could block regulatory reforms, adding that socially, very real public fatigue over reform and distributional concerns -- especially in communities dependent on legacy industries -- risks backlash.
"Finally, external shocks (energy price volatility, global economic slowdown) could divert attention and funding, making sequencing, credible commitments, and strong delivery institutions essential," she added.

People in Latvia will be able to “ban” themselves from taking out loans – parliament adopts major changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
13:17:36 UTC
22:17:36 KST

The Latvian parliament on Thursday adopted amendments to the Consumer Rights Protection Law giving consumers the right to indicate through credit information bureaus that they do not wish to take out loans. Lenders will be required to take this into account when assessing credit applications.
The amendments are intended to promote responsible lending, provide more effective protection against excessive debt and fraud, and make the lending environment clearer, more transparent and better suited to modern needs.
The changes also introduce new rules for cases in which loan repayments are overdue. Lenders will be allowed to impose only justified and proportionate charges and, before initiating debt collection, will be required to seek less burdensome solutions and provide information about available debt counselling services.
The amendments prohibit the granting of unsolicited credit – a credit product that a consumer has neither requested nor agreed to receive. Lenders will also be required to inform consumers promptly when they exceed their credit limit, including details of any associated fees and interest. If such overdrafts occur regularly, lenders will have to provide information about more favourable alternatives and opportunities to obtain debt counselling.
In certain cases, lenders offering instalment loans and “buy now, pay later” products will also be required to assess the consumer’s ability to repay the loan.
The amendments also introduce clearer rules for digital lending. Before concluding a contract remotely, lenders will have to provide information in an easily understandable format, offer a simple way to withdraw from the agreement and present information in a manner that is easy to understand online. If a credit offer is personalised using automated data processing or artificial intelligence, consumers will have to be informed.
Consumers will also have the right to request human involvement in automated decisions concerning credit applications and to receive a clear explanation of why their application was approved or rejected.
In addition, registration requirements for credit intermediaries will be expanded, while registration requirements will also be introduced for large companies that provide credit in the form of deferred payments.
The amendments also introduce a new product – an equity-release loan. This will allow a person to obtain a loan secured against real estate that is not their primary residence, such as a second unused apartment. The loan may amount to no more than 70% of the property’s market value. Such loans will be available to people aged 21 and over, with a maximum repayment period of 30 years.
On Thursday, the Saeima also adopted related amendments to the Credit Information Bureaus Law.

Battle for UP's 'Aadhi Aabadi': Why parties are wooing women voters like never before ahead of 2027 polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

13:16:37 UTC
22:16:37 KST

Battle for UP's 'Aadhi Aabadi': Why parties are wooing women voters like never before ahead of 2027 polls
Priyanka Mukherjee / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 20, 2026, 18:48 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Why UP's 'Aadhi Aabadi' matters more than ever in the 2027 election
NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh elections have traditionally been about the caste arithmetic: counting Yadavs, non-Yadav OBCs, Dalits, Brahmins and Muslims. But ahead of the 2027 battle, there is another constituency the parties simply cannot afford to ignore: the women voters - who transcend the caste divide.Every election cycle, the same questions return: Can the BJP retain its non-Yadav OBC votes? Will Akhilesh Yadav manage to woo Brahmins and Dalits? Which side will the Jatav voters pick? Will Mayawati be able to rally all Dalits behind her BSP? And so on.This time around, while the caste questions remain, the battle will also be for the support of Uttar Pradesh's 'Aadhi Aabadi' - the women voters who have proved to be game changers, election after election in many other states.When Uttar Pradesh votes in 2027 to elect a new assembly, the state's 6,09,09,525 female voters, who constitute 45.46% of the total electorate, will hold considerable sway over the fortunes of the political contenders.That explains why Yogi Adityanath and Akhilesh Yadav, the two key challengers, are leaving no stone unturned to bring women into their fold. Congress, too, is preparing to step up its outreach as the electoral battle gathers pace.
Why women voters matter
Let's rewind to 2007. In the 2007 UP assembly election, the female turnout in the state was under 42%, less than the male turnout of 49.35%.But this changed five years later. In 2012, Uttar Pradesh had around 5.72 crore registered women voters, of whom 3.45 crore cast their ballots. Thus, the female turnout increased to around 60.3%, surpassing that of males at about 58.7%.By the 2017 assembly election, the number of registered women voters had gone up to 6.46 crore. More than 4.09 crore women voted, and female turnout climbed to around 63.4% while the men lagged at 59%.In 2022, Uttar Pradesh had around 7.02 crore women electors, out of which more than 4.36 crore voted. Female turnout stood at around 62.2%, once again higher than that among men, which stood at around 59.6%.So, between 2012 and 2022 alone, the state added nearly 1.3 crore women to its electoral rolls. But what may be more important for political parties is the fact that 2012 elections onwards women outvoted men in all assembly elections in the state. The 2024 Lok Sabha election was no different.In Uttar Pradesh, 57.22% of women electors turned out to vote in the 2024 general elections, compared to 56.46% of men. The overall turnout was lower than in the recent assembly elections, but women still maintained their lead.And it’s not just UP. Parties cannot ignore the decisive role women voters have played in assembly elections in Bihar, Maharashtra, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand.Ahead of the assembly election in Madhya Pradesh, the Shivraj Singh Chouhan government rolled out the 'Ladli Behna' programme, a monthly cash assistance scheme under which money was transferred directly into women's accounts. By the time Madhya Pradesh voted, the scheme covered more than a crore women. BJP won 163 of the 230 seats. 'Ladli Behna' quickly became one of the key takeaways from the election.Maharashtra also introduced its own version: the 'Ladki Bahin' programme. And then Bihar happened. The 2025 assembly election recorded a female turnout of 71.6%. Male turnout was 62.8%. The NDA went on to win a huge majority.
How parties are wooing women voters
Financial doles under DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) no longer make news. If the elections are round the corner, they are a given. What makes news is the amount of dole.So, when some media reports suggested that the Yogi Adityanath government was considering a dole of Rs 50,000 for women ahead of elections - Rs 20,000 now and Rs 30,000 after its return to power - Akhilesh Yadav lost no time to dish out a pre-election offer to counter the BJP. “We will start with Rs 40,000 and increase it every year,” the SP chief wrote in a post on X while questioning the BJP’s intent and alleging that the BJP was distributing "the earnings of its sins."Akhilesh simultaneously launched a broadside against the BJP and alleged that the party has been left with "nothing but money" to win the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections. “The religious women of UP will never accept the ill-gotten money of the BJP,” the SP chief wrote. He also tried to discredit the BJP and claimed that the party was not keeping its promise of giving the announced doles to women in other states where it governed."The BJP's corrupt government has eaten up Rs 5 lakh belonging to women over the last 10 years and is now serving the jumla of giving only Rs 20,000. Rs 20,000 is only four per cent of Rs 5 lakh, which means these BJP people have swallowed 96 per cent of women's share," he alleged.BJP Uttar Pradesh vice-president Neeraj Singh hit back at Akhilesh, saying his party has made no such announcement and accused the SP chief of making a "deceptive" promise to give Rs 40,000 to women."Whenever the BJP provides benefits under its schemes to eligible people, the important thing is that the money reaches those who are entitled to it. The distribution system is also very transparent, and this has been the BJP's track record," the BJP leader claimed.On the SP's promise of Rs 40,000 annually to women, Singh said it was "only a deception" and alleged that the party had used a similar tactic before the 2024 Lok Sabha elections.But while the BJP questions Akhilesh Yadav’s sincerity, it perhaps realises that the SP chief has raised the bar and also the expectation of women in the state by announcing a dole of Rs 40,000, and this announcement may influence whatever dole the ruling party eventually decides.Akhilesh may have scored some brownie points here, but the fact remains that the SP chief faces a tough challenge from the BJP in UP. Chief minister Yogi Adityanath has been in a relentless pursuit of women voters, announcing a string of programmes for them at regular intervals.In March, Yogi Adityanath distributed smartphones to 69,804 Anganwadi workers and supervisors, over two lakh growth monitoring devices, and appointment letters to 18,440 Anganwadi workers and helpers. Addressing the gathering, he said, "If the newborn is well-nourished and the mother is healthy, the future of India will be strong."In April, the Uttar Pradesh government launched a one-of-its-kind scheme titled 'Safe Mobility Program,' centred around employment generation for female members of Self-Help Groups (SHGs). Under the programme, an army of female e-rickshaw pilots will be trained across the state to ensure safe, accessible, and dignified transportation for girls and women travelling to schools, workplaces, and other essential destinations.From April 16 to 20, the Yogi government ran a five-day special campaign under the Nari Shakti Vandan Abhiyan to turn schools into active centres of women empowerment, focusing on building confidence, leadership qualities, and awareness among girl students.In another move to support and prop up 'naari shakti', the Uttar Pradesh government directed sugarcane co-operative societies in the state to allocate free spaces to women from Self Help Groups (SHGs) to set up their shops. The idea was to encourage women from SHGs to start ‘Prerna canteens’ from here, displaying and selling their products.These are some examples that showcase how Yogi Adityanath has been mindful of the power of women voters in the 2027 battle and has been working to reach out to them through his welfare measures.
Congress's another shot at wooing women voters
BJP and Samajwadi Party are not the only parties to target this demographic. Congress had, in fact, put women at the centre of its Uttar Pradesh campaign much before the current race over cash transfers began. In 2022, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, who was the general secretary of the All India Congress Committee (AICC) in charge of Uttar Pradesh back then, led the party's 'Ladki Hoon, Lad Sakti Hoon' campaign. The party took a bold gamble by promising to give 40% of assembly tickets to women.The party eventually fielded a large number of women candidates and also made promises aimed specifically at female voters, including smartphones for girls and electric scooters for female students. However, that move did not pay off. Congress won just two of the 403 assembly seats and its vote share slipped to around 2.3%.The situation, however, is different going into 2027. Congress won six Lok Sabha seats in Uttar Pradesh in 2024 as part of its alliance with the Samajwadi Party, which won 37. The opposition therefore enters the assembly battle with more political space than it had in 2022. For Congress, the challenge will be to revive its women outreach and aim to translate schemes into electoral benefit.
Women are voting more, but are they voting as one bloc?
But amid all the attention on cash transfers and the push for women-centric schemes, the question that remains is: Can women's votes be treated as one single bloc? A Jatav woman, a Muslim woman, a non-Yadav OBC woman may have very different expectations when she enters the polling booth to cast her vote. Caste, religion and past preferences may still continue to matter, as will factors like inflation, jobs, law and order, women's safety, welfare benefits and the candidate on the ground.
Therefore, it is hard to predict if the high turnout among women can automatically translate into an advantage for any one party.But what it does surely mean is that no party can afford to take the 'Aadhi Aabadi' for granted anymore. When it comes to voting, women have outperformed men in the last three Uttar Pradesh assembly elections and have maintained that lead in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls as well. So, while caste will always play a role in UP elections, the 2027 battle will also come down to who wins the trust of the over six crore women voters. The question is no longer whether women will turn up to vote. It is: who will they vote for?
Priyanka Mukherjee is an Assistant News Editor at The Times of India, where deadlines rarely slow down. Often juggling breaking news, long-form explainers and the everyday chaos of the newsroom, she is usually managing stress, chasing clarity and trying to log off on time (rarely successful). She also cares deeply about stories around women’s rights and social change, while two very opinionated dogs make sure she never truly switches off.

Meta 'knew and did nothing,' whistleblower reveals in child safety trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
13:16:09 UTC
22:16:09 KST

Prosecutors have claimed that Meta was aware of the damage its platforms did to young users' mental health, but chose to hide it and keep harvesting their data.
Meta is currently undergoing a landmark trial in Oakland, California, litigated by four US states — Colorado, California, New Jersey and Kentucky. The case could permanently change how popular social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram are designed.
The states accuse the social media giant of intentionally designing its platforms to addict younger users and hiding what it knew about the harmful effects on their mental health, claims Meta has consistently denied.
The trial, which started on Tuesday, has been called the largest consumer protection lawsuit in American history by Kentucky's attorney general, Russell Coleman.
Testimony in the trial's first three days has already produced striking claims about what Meta knew and when.
Whistleblower Arturo Béjar, a former Meta engineering director, testified that the company's public Community Standards Enforcement Reports — which measure how often users are shown content that violates Meta's policies — could be understating the real risk by as much as 100 times, based on internal user surveys that asked people directly about their negative experiences on the platforms.
'Hook, harvest, hide'
California's deputy attorney general, Megan O'Neill, told jurors in her opening statement that Meta's business model could be summed up in four words: "Hook the users. Hold them for as long as they can. Harvest their data. Hide the truth from the public when making public statements."
She alleged that Meta hid the truth about the real risks of its platforms for younger users in an attempt to hook them and harvest their data, and accused the company of actively intervening in its own mental health research to further obscure those risks.
Meta's lawyer, Paul Schmidt, argued in response that the tech giant has a track record of sharing information about social media harms, and that enforcing content and age-limit policies is complicated. Verifying a user's age through documents such as government identification or credit cards, he said, poses its own problems, since not every user has access to either.
Schmidt also said Meta's employees are working on improving the platforms' impact on user wellbeing, and urged the jury to keep an open mind.
Prosecutors also argued that Meta was aware large numbers of children under 13 were active on Instagram despite the platform's rules.
Béjar testified that his own research had uncovered tens of thousands of under-13 users, while Meta's own technology was capable of flagging potentially millions more.
Rather than pushing to remove them, he said, the company's approach was effectively "don't ask, don't tell."
Béjar told jurors that despite repeated warnings, Meta continued to treat safety as an afterthought — including during the rollout of major features such as Reels, where he said "safety was not a consideration in how it was initially deployed."
He described emailing Chris Cox, Meta's chief product officer, to flag what he saw as a stark gap between the harm users were reporting and what the company was prioritising and telling the public.
Béjar has previously said that in an earlier conversation, Cox was the first Meta executive who could answer, off the top of his head, what percentage of users were experiencing this kind of harm — a moment Béjar described as "heartbreaking," because it meant Meta's leadership already knew and had chosen not to act.
Meta primarily measures harm on its platforms through the prevalence of content that violates its own policies.
Béjar rejected this metric outright. Citing the example of a 13-year-old sharing distress and asking for help, he told the court: "Harm is what people experience as harm. Prevalence is a very narrow measure of a very specific thing."
He also said Instagram had shifted from a platform users actively chose to use, to one that increasingly used them — largely because its feed evolved from showing mostly people users followed to showing mostly strangers, a change he said introduced substantial new risks.
The outcome of the trial could have ripple effects well beyond Meta. Because the case rests on the argument that a platform's interface and design choices — not just individual pieces of content — can create legal liability, a ruling against Meta could shape how rivals such as Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube approach the same questions.

A sea drone destroyed by the Romanian military using onboard cannon fire from a Romanian F-16 near the Neptun Deep gas platform in the Black Sea was not Ukrainian, Romania’s Defense Ministry said.
"Through a recently established direct communication channel with the Ukrainian side, we received official confirmation that it is not of Ukrainian origin," the ministry said on Facebook.
The ministry explained that the coast guard detected the drone a few hundred meters from the site of gas extraction operations at the Neptun Deep platform, in the exclusive economic zone, 80 miles east of Constanta.
"An operational headquarters was set up at the Defense Ministry, which asked NATO to hand over command to the Romanian military. Following analysis and in coordination with Romania’s president, a decision was made to destroy the drone in order to protect the lives of several hundred people working on the platform and to ensure the security of critical infrastructure," the ministry explained.
Two Romanian F-16 fighter jets were scrambled to respond, with orders to open fire. The drone was safely destroyed.

Swiss insurers’ profits jumped in 2025
The financial situation of the Swiss insurance sector is “generally sound”, according to a report by the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) published on Thursday. Insurers significantly increased their capital last year.
According to the FINMA report, Swiss insurance companies posted an aggregate annual profit of CHF24.4 billion ($30.6 billion) in 2025, up 136% year-on-year from CHF14 billion.
Annual profits for non-life insurers and reinsurers rose particularly sharply, reaching CHF12.9 billion and CHF9.8 billion respectively. Life insurers also saw their aggregate annual profit rise by 10.2% to CHF1.7 billion.
FINMA notes that investments were one of the factors contributing to these results. Across the market as a whole, investment profits rose by 47.6% to CHF24.8 billion. Their return stood at 5%, compared with 3.37% the previous year.
+ Is Switzerland’s natural disaster insurance a model for the world?
As regards gross premiums, their aggregate volume fell slightly to CHF149 billion (-0.6 per cent). The trend varied across sectors: life insurers and non-life insurers saw their gross premiums rise by 3.7% and 2.8% respectively, while reinsurers experienced a decline of 6.1%. This was mainly due to the appreciation of the Swiss franc against the US dollar, the euro and the pound sterling.

Danish and Russian drones observe each other in Baltic Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
13:13:32 UTC
22:13:32 KST

- A Russian corvette and reconnaissance drone approached a Danish uncrewed surface vessel near Bornholm on June 25, with each side observing the other.
- Stormborn's X-Wave 01 recorded the encounter with radar and cameras and handed the data to the Royal Danish Navy.
A Danish uncrewed surface vessel and a Russian reconnaissance drone spent several minutes observing each other near Bornholm in the Baltic Sea on June 25, after the Russian corvette Soobrazitelny approached the Danish drone at close range.
The Stormborn X-Wave 01 was anchored about 30 kilometers (19 miles) southeast of Bornholm, testing radar and sonar equipment supplied by Danish defense manufacturers Terma and Mydefence, according to Stormborn and reporting by Danish broadcaster TV 2. The Soobrazitelny, a Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette with hull number 531, passed within roughly 200 meters of the Danish vessel with its Automatic Identification System transponder switched off.
The corvette then launched a small quadcopter drone that circled the Danish boat at close range for several minutes, according to Stormborn.
Stormborn founder and CEO Frederik Søndergaard Hansen said the company had positioned the drone in an area with limited Danish coastal radar coverage.
“We lay down there to monitor an area that the Danish Defence has a hard time keeping an eye on,” Hansen said.
“I would say that this is the first time that it has succeeded in image documenting a drone so close to Danish territory,” Hansen said.
The Stormborn vessel’s onboard sensors tracked the corvette throughout the encounter, identifying it by radar, electro-optical and infrared cameras, and detecting the Russian drone through radio-frequency sensors, according to Stormborn. The company said its artificial intelligence system correctly identified the corvette’s hull number and tagged crew members visible on deck along with a Ka-27 helicopter parked on the ship’s landing pad.
Stormborn said it handed all radar logs, sensor data and video footage from the encounter to the Royal Danish Navy’s maritime surveillance service. TV 2 published the footage and radar plots in mid-July.
Footage recorded by the Russian quadcopter itself has since surfaced, showing the drone’s view as it circled the Danish vessel. The video gives a rare look at the encounter from both sides, with the Stormborn footage showing the Russian drone and corvette, and the Russian footage showing the Danish boat below.
The Soobrazitelny has been observed on previous occasions escorting tankers associated with Russia’s shadow fleet and was seen doing so again in the days following the Bornholm encounter.
The Steregushchiy-class corvette displaces roughly 2,100 tons, measures 104.5 meters (343 feet) in length, and carries a crew of about 100, according to publicly available naval specifications. The Stormborn X-Wave is a small uncrewed surface vessel designed to be towed by road and deployed without a crew for extended offshore monitoring.

DHAKA, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, candidate of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), was elected Bangladesh's 23rd president in a presidential election held on Thursday, Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) AMM Nasir Uddin announced.
Alamgir secured 255 votes, while his rival Oli Ahmad, chairman of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and candidate of the alliance led by Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, received 88 votes.
Voting was held in the chamber of the Jatiya Sangsad, or parliament, from 2 p.m. to 5 p.m. local time. A total of 349 members of parliament were eligible to vote, and 343 valid votes were cast.
The president of Bangladesh is elected by members of parliament. The ruling BNP currently holds an absolute majority in parliament.
The presidential election was held to fill the vacancy left by former President Mohammed Shahabuddin Chuppu, who tendered his resignation on July 24. Under the country's Constitution, a new president must be elected within 90 days after the office falls vacant.
The newly elected president is scheduled to take the oath of office on Friday evening. ■

Exclusive: An Iraqi faction handed over drones, missile to govt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
13:12:55 UTC
22:12:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: An Iraqi faction handed over drones and missiles to the government
A senior Iraqi official in Baghdad told The New Arab on Wednesday, 19 August, that an armed faction had handed over several drones and missiles with a range of more than 100 kilometres to the Iraqi government in the presence of US representatives.
The handover took place at a site near Baghdad several days ago, as part of Iraqi government efforts to make convincing progress for the United States, which has threatened to impose economic and financial sanctions on Iraq if Iran-aligned groups continue to retain their own weapons arsenals.
The Iraqi government continues to conceal a large part of the file concerning the state monopoly on weapons, including the mechanism for receiving and handing over weapons and the type of weapons handed over, as part of internal understandings to stem political disputes.
The positions of the 69 armed factions regarding surrendering their weapons to the Iraqi government vary. All are affiliated with the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), but a large proportion of them are connected to this umbrella only through receiving monthly salaries.
The main factions most closely linked to the Iranian Revolutionary Guard continue to refuse to hand over their weapons and threatened to confront the government if it decides to resort to force.
They have announced conditions that observers describe as impossible to meet, most notably the withdrawal of US and Turkish forces, the dissolution of the Peshmerga forces, Iraq having control over its political, economic and financial decisions, and the expulsion of US companies from the country.
These positions were set out in statements and comments issued in recent weeks by Kataib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba, Kataib al-Awfiya and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada.
Other factions, most notably Al-Badala, Badr and Al-Tufuf, have remained silent.
On Wednesday, a senior Iraqi security official told The New Arab that an armed faction, which has a political wing and a parliamentary bloc, had voluntarily handed over about 20 Iranian-made fixed-wing drones to the government.
The handover took place in the presence of US representatives, who observed the process at a site outside Baghdad.
He explained that the drones were one-way suicide aircraft with ranges of more than 250 kilometres, powered by fuel engines, and that the process was filmed.
The Iraqi official said the weapons targeted for disarmament were drones and cross-border missiles with ranges of more than 100 kilometres since the US was not concerned with conventional weapons such as artillery, mortars and machine guns.
None of the factions responding to the state weapons monopoly initiative has announced the types of weapons they have handed over to the state.
The most prominent of these factions are Saraya al-Salam, the military wing of the Sadrist movement led by Muqtada al-Sadr, and Asaib Ahl al-Haq, led by Qais al-Khazali, which announced it had severed its brigades' affiliation.
Some of its leaders are involved in procedures to hand over weapons or place them at the disposal of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, the head of government.
Kataib Imam Ali, led by Shibl al-Zaydi, also chose to sever its military affiliation and placed some of its capabilities under the command of the head of government.
Many questions remain over the types, nature and effectiveness of the weapons. And so far, no one has responded to numerous reports claiming that the weapons were nothing more than "scrap".
But The New Arab has obtained new information concerning the type of weapons from a senior commander in an Iraqi faction that handed over its weapons to the state.
"The process of bringing the factions' weapons under state control is not as complicated as is being portrayed in the media or in political and security analysis," the senior commander said. "Bringing the weapons under state control means drones whose range reaches the occupied Palestinian territories."
"One of the factions handed over this type of aircraft in a process involving Iraqi forces and representatives of the faction itself, in the presence of personnel affiliated with the US Embassy," he added. "These personnel filmed the handover and the blessing of this transformation."
The commander, who refused to disclose his identity, noted: "The Iraqi factions have all types of weapons possessed by the Iraqi army, except for warplanes. Some have modern and advanced technologies for monitoring and tracking air and military movements. The majority of these weapons and technologies are imported from Iran as part of Iran providing the factions with expertise through Iranian advisers and officers who have been working in Iraq for more than a decade."
"These technologies increased during the war against Islamic State and continued to expand after 2020, particularly after the assassination of Qassem Soleimani and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis," he continued.
"At that point, Iran provided its allied factions with significant human, technical and training resources, specifically Harakat al-Nujaba, Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada and Kataib Hezbollah. Therefore, the weapons possessed by these factions cannot be considered scrap or ordinary. They are advanced and important, which is why they refuse to hand them over in any way."
"Harakat al-Nujaba categorically refuses to hand over its weapons and is relying on the Iranian role to suppress the campaign to bring weapons under state control in Iraq through Iranian officials who have visited Iraq in recent weeks," added the commander.
"The latest was parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who, in the first moments after arriving in Baghdad, made comments supporting the resistance factions in a clear challenge to the authority of Iraq, which is moving towards restricting and curbing the role of the factions. As for Kataib Hezbollah, it has held more than one meeting with government and judicial council officials. Despite the tensions, the talks are continuing at a slow pace," he said.
Regarding the factions' headquarters or weapons depots, the commander said, "The faction leaders are keen not to talk about their headquarters or the tunnels they possess. This file is extremely secret, and even some Iranian leaders do not know about them."
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf made an official visit to Iraq on Wednesday, 19 August, as US pressure intensified on the Tehran-allied factions of the Popular Mobilisation Forces.
The visit occurs amid tense regional conditions and deteriorating relations between Iran and Arab neighbouring countries.
Upon arriving at Baghdad International Airport, Ghalibaf went directly to the site where Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani, a former commander of Iran's Revolutionary Guard, was assassinated. Soleimani was killed in a US airstrike in 2020 that targeted him immediately after he arrived in Baghdad from Damascus, accompanied by Popular Mobilisation Forces commander Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis.
"The resistance in Iraq has become an essential element of global power," the Iranian parliament speaker had said.
Ghalibaf's comments angered supporters of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and his campaign to monopolise weapons under the state.
At the same time, Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, spokesman for Kataib Hezbollah, issued a harsh address to al-Zaidi following the arrest of Abbas al-Yacoubi, the intelligence official of Harakat al-Nujaba, describing the Iraqi PM as a "young man" and that "our patience is running out".
Describing the 100 days of al-Zaidi's government as "empty genius from the young Ali al-Zeidi", al-Assaf also said the Iraqi PM must "understand the governing equations and listen to the advice of the elderly politicians."
"However, we have not seen any development in his understanding of the complex circumstances facing Iraq and the region. Rather, he has made matters worse by insisting on listening to the advice of US envoy Thomas Barrack," he added.
Ali Fadlallah, a political affairs researcher close to the Iraqi factions, said, "There are those who want to drag the state and the factions into a battle. Otherwise, what does it mean to arrest and terrorise the families of fighters through attacks and unjustified arrests in a crazy manner that no Iraqi with dignity and the right to live safely in his country can accept?"
"Anyone who says they know the types of weapons possessed by the factions is speaking without understanding because the factions deal with this issue with a high degree of secrecy," he told The New Arab. "As for the sources of the weapons, most are Iraqi or arrived in Iraq through many channels. The factions that handed over their weapons have not abandoned the idea of resistance, but the situation in Iraq requires pragmatic thinking rather than relying on force and hardline positions."
"The factions that handed over their weapons have cleared themselves before the Iraqi state of any attacks that might target Americans or facilities accused of dealing with the Israeli enemy in Iraqi areas," Fadlallah added. "But the factions that refuse to hand over their weapons believe that Iraq is still effectively occupied, as foreign forces continue to have a malign role on Iraqi soil. Moreover, Iraqi decision-making is still influenced by US directives, and this is unacceptable."
Meanwhile, Iraqi security affairs researcher Sarmad al-Bayati said, "The Iraqi government appears firmly serious, without retreat, about resolving the issue of the factions. The measures it is taking are moving in an escalatory direction to establish security and stability and enforce the law through containment, pursuit and arrests.
"Therefore, the factions feel this danger and appear agitated in their latest statements, even though the Coordination Framework, the ruling Shia alliance, wants the process of bringing weapons under state control to continue through understanding and calm," he added.
He ruled out that "the situation is currently considered under control and that the possibility of confrontation between the two sides is currently unlikely, but the situation is generally unsettling."

China to host World Cleanup Day global observance in Shaoxing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
21:12:48 CST
22:12:48 KST

HANGZHOU, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- The global observance of World Cleanup Day 2026 will be held in Shaoxing City, east China's Zhejiang Province, marking the first time China has been chosen to host the event.
Cecilia Andersson, Programme Management Officer and Waste Management Lead at UN-Habitat, announced at a press conference in Shaoxing on Thursday that the event, themed "From Clean Plates to Clean Cities," will run from Sept. 19 to 21.
Andersson noted that preventing and reducing waste at the source contributes to building cleaner, healthier and more resource-efficient cities.
"Hosting the event allows us to learn from practices worldwide, while driving cities toward high-quality development and creating better living spaces for people," said Wang Shengjun, chief economist at the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development.
Wang said the goals and principles of World Cleanup Day closely align with China's efforts to build modern, people-centered cities.
The host city Shaoxing, an early practitioner of the nationwide "Clean Your Plate" campaign, has been actively promoting grassroots green initiatives, including household waste sorting and citywide cleanup drives.
In 2021, for example, the city rolled out an action plan to curb food waste, mobilizing all sectors to make Shaoxing a model of thrift and foster a culture of conservation.
The global event comes as China steps up its nationwide efforts in waste management and environmental cleanup. Earlier in January, China released an action plan to significantly expand its solid waste treatment capacity over the next five years, as part of broader efforts to advance a comprehensive green transition across the economy and society.
Meanwhile, China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) outlines initiatives for comprehensive solid waste treatment, stronger environmental risk controls, and significant progress in addressing emerging pollutants.
Established by the United Nations General Assembly in 2023, World Cleanup Day is observed annually on Sept. 20. It aims to raise public awareness of the role cleanup efforts play in sustainable development.
Previous editions have addressed a wide range of global environmental issues, from the challenges of waste pollution in polar regions to efforts targeting textile and fashion waste. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- China has become Ecuador's second-largest trading partner as bilateral trade has grown rapidly since the China-Ecuador free trade agreement (FTA) took effect more than two years ago, a commerce ministry spokesperson said Thursday.
Bilateral trade reached 9.83 billion U.S. dollars in the first half of this year, up more than 20 percent year on year, spokesperson He Yadong told a regular press conference.
On Tuesday, China's Ministry of Commerce and Ecuador's ministry of economic and productive development signed a roadmap for bilateral economic and trade cooperation and a memorandum of understanding on supporting free trade and multilateralism, witnessed by the two heads of state, He said.
The two sides agreed to strengthen economic and trade coordination and advance cooperation in areas such as trade and investment, agriculture and food, e-commerce and sustainable development, according to the spokesperson.
They will also work together to implement the bilateral FTA, avoid taking unjustified discriminatory economic and trade measures against each other, and maintain communication and share information on trade measures involving third countries, the spokesperson said.
China is ready to work with Ecuador to implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, make good use of bilateral economic and trade cooperation mechanisms, promote higher-quality China-Ecuador economic and trade cooperation, and further deepen and advance the China-Ecuador comprehensive strategic partnership, said He. ■

KUALA LUMPUR, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's labor productivity per hour worked rose 5.5 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, accelerating from 4.8 percent growth in the previous quarter, official data showed Thursday.
Value added per hour worked increased to 46.50 ringgit from 45.50 ringgit in the first quarter, supported by a 6 percent expansion in economic activity, the Department of Statistics Malaysia said in a statement.
Total hours worked rose 0.5 percent to 9.6 billion hours.
Labor productivity measured by value added per employment grew 4.9 percent year-on-year, compared with 4.3 percent in the first quarter.
Value added per employee increased to 26,595 ringgit from 26,168 ringgit, while total employment rose 1.1 percent to 16.8 million.
Sustained productivity gains would remain crucial to improving economic efficiency, competitiveness and long-term growth, it said. (1 ringgit equals 0.25 USD) ■

China Focus: Robot conference spotlights commercial push for China's robot sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
21:12:25 CST
22:12:25 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- At an exhibition hall, about 10 humanoid robots worked in a coordinated workflow, with some lifting and stacking boxes and others sorting goods along an assembly line. Together, they demonstrated a complete smart logistics process -- from material handling to sorting and replenishment.
This scene, presented by humanoid robot maker UBTECH at the 2026 World Robot Conference (WRC) in Beijing, conveys one message: robots are quickly evolving from showpieces to real-world applications.
The conference, which runs from Wednesday through Sunday, has drawn more than 300 exhibitors from 26 countries, with over 3,000 products on display, including more than 300 debuts.
At the Galaxea display area, visitors scanned a QR code to order a bottle of water. A robot autonomously navigated through the warehouse to fetch and package the water in just over one minute, relying solely on model-based recognition. This system is already up and running in Beijing and other cities.
"The solution can solve overnight warehouse staffing problems," said Luo Tianqi, chief financial officer of Galaxea. "Nighttime order volumes aren't huge, but still require people on night shifts. Replacing them with robots is economically viable."
China's humanoid robot industry is entering a critical stage of large-scale commercialization and deployment, as embodied intelligence products move from small-batch trials to broader adoption, Xu Xiaolan, chairwoman of the Chinese Institute of Electronics, said at the 2026 WRC.
Nearly 10 major automakers, including BYD and SAIC, are already testing embodied-intelligence systems on production lines for tasks like material handling and parts loading. Embodied-intelligence robots are also operating in high-risk, confined spaces for disaster relief, flood response and hazardous industrial inspections, Xu added.
Unitree Robotics founder and CEO Wang Xingxing said at the conference that the company's robots are already being tested on auto assembly lines and in its own factories, with AI research focused on improving their ability to perform practical tasks in homes and industrial environments.
On Wednesday, the Hangzhou-based company became the first humanoid robot maker listed on the A-share market, marking a significant step for the country's humanoid robot industry.
This year's conference has also emphasized industrial chain collaboration. The WRC brings together AI algorithm developers, 3D-vision and battery suppliers, robot makers and end-users to facilitate cooperation and shorten R&D and iteration cycles.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, revenue for China's robotics sector exceeded 300 billion yuan (about 44.24 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, with average annual growth of over 20 percent in the past five years. In the first half of 2026, revenue reached 165.5 billion yuan, up 24.5 percent year on year.
Chinese robots have demonstrated their technological prowess through impressive feats, ranging from martial arts to marathons. Meanwhile, China is doubling down on expanding robots' real-world applications, despite predictions that the industry's "GPT moment" remains years away.
Across the country, China has already built more than 70 embodied-intelligence training grounds as of June, with 46 more under construction or being planned, according to a report by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology.
The industry has benefited from supportive national strategy. "Embodied intelligence" was first written into China's government work report in 2025. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for a forward-looking layout of future industries, including embodied artificial intelligence, as well as mechanisms to boost funding and share risks in these emerging sectors.
Wang said "a ChatGPT moment in embodied intelligence" will come when robots can be dropped into unfamiliar settings and complete most tasks via simple voice or text commands. He expects that such a breakthrough could occur within two to three years in an optimistic scenario, or within five to ten years at the latest. ■

Across China: Tibetan medical thangkas draw global spotlight at symposium in Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
21:12:23 CST
22:12:23 KST

LHASA, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- An international symposium opened in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Thursday to shed light on the growing global interest in traditional Tibetan medicine and its visual illustrations drawn on thangkas.
Held in the regional capital Lhasa, the second international academic symposium on "The Four Treatises of Tibetan Medicine" and Tibetan medical thangkas brought together more than 200 experts from China, Britain, Germany, Austria, Mongolia and Nepal.
Discussions centered on the historical evolution of the classic treatises, the iconographic interpretation of Tibetan medical thangkas, and pathways for modern clinical application and international cooperation.
At the symposium, a research center for Tibetan medical thangkas was inaugurated.
Written between the 8th and 12th centuries, "The Four Treatises of Tibetan Medicine" is the most influential foundational work on traditional Tibetan medicine. It was inscribed on the UNESCO Memory of the World Register in 2023.
Based on the work, the 80-scroll Tibetan medical thangkas serve as a visual teaching complement, covering diagnostics, pharmacology, preventive care and medical ethics. The medical thangkas were added to China's national documentary heritage list also in 2023.
Among the participants was Katharina Anna Sabernig, a lecturer from the Medical University of Vienna, Austria, who first encountered Tibetan medical murals at Labrang Monastery in Gansu Province in 1994. She later returned and began delving deeper into the works.
"I saw these murals and I started to get deeper and deeper and to understand all this," Sabernig recalled.
Mary Caroline Wyatt, a scholar with dual British-Greek citizenship, began collaborating on an English translation of texts about Tibetan medical thangkas last September. She noted that complete English versions have long been scarce.
"Our translations target professional readers so that we preserve many specialized, traditional terms," said Wyatt.
The event was hosted by the regional health commission and co-organized by the regional Tibetan medicine hospital and Xizang University of Tibetan Medicine.
Xizang has formulated and implemented a series of policies on promoting Tibetan medicine and encouraging innovation. According to a government white paper released last year, the region has 51 public Tibetan medicine institutions, employing 5,287 professionals and operating 3,260 beds, up from 28 institutions, 2,232 professionals and 1,364 beds in 2012.
In April, China rolled out its first national recommended standard for ethnic-medicine disease classification and codes for Tibetan medicine.
Tsering, president of the regional Tibetan medicine hospital, said inscriptions on the UNESCO Memory of the World Register and China's national documentary heritage list have brought Tibetan medicine to a broader global audience.
"We will make the most of these opportunities to promote academic exchanges and clinical collaboration worldwide," Tsering said. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has approved a two-year commercial trial of satellite Internet of Things (IoT) services by Zhejiang Geespace Technology Co., Ltd., marking the latest step in opening the sector to private companies.
During the two-year trial, Geespace will provide wide-area, low-power and reliable IoT connectivity services, enabling round-the-clock smart data collection and remote interaction in sectors such as smart transportation, marine fisheries, energy and water conservancy, the ministry said on Thursday.
Satellite IoT uses satellite networks to connect devices and vehicles such as data terminals, wearable devices, cars, ships and aircraft, particularly in areas where terrestrial networks have limited coverage.
The latest approval comes as China seeks to expand the commercial applications of satellite communications and develop its commercial space industry.
The country launched commercial trials of satellite IoT services in November 2025. In May of this year, Beijing Guodian Gaoke Technology Co., Ltd. received approval to conduct a two-year commercial trial.
Commercial trials are expected to help satellite IoT services achieve economies of scale and promote more coordinated industry development, the ministry said.
For years, basic telecommunications licences in the satellite communication sector have largely been held by major state-owned companies, while private firms have mainly operated in satellite manufacturing, launch services and downstream applications.
A policy document issued by China's State Council in November 2025 called for equal treatment of private investment projects in commercial spaceflight frequency licensing and launch approvals.
China will further optimize market access for satellite communications and strengthen regulation and security across the industry chain to promote the sector's development, according to the ministry. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: 18 years later, American basketball player Myron Allen finds his way back to Xinjiang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
21:12:14 CST
22:12:14 KST

by sportswriter Sun Zhe
URUMQI, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- A summer rain had just fallen over Urumqi when Myron Allen stepped onto a basketball court he had not seen in 18 years. Inside the brightly lit gym, the 47-year-old American guard was doing what he had done countless times before: working with young players and showing them how to attack off the dribble.
The city has changed since Allen first arrived in 2008. But the basketball court feels familiar. So does the work.
Standing 1.8 meters tall, Allen was never the biggest player on the court. During a professional career that took him to countries including Mexico, Venezuela and Australia, he built his reputation on speed and athleticism.
Yet of all the places he has played, Allen says Xinjiang remains the one that feels most like home.
"I don't know why, but in my heart it just felt warm," he said. "Sometimes I go somewhere and just say goodbye. But here, I feel like I'm with family."
A BOLD CHOICE
When Allen arrived in 2008, Xinjiang basketball was still searching for recognition. The roster did not include any member of China's national team, while its best-known player, former NBA champion Mengke Bateer, was already 33.
Allen still remembers how unexpectedly the opportunity came.
"One night at around 10 p.m., I was about to go to sleep when I got a phone call asking if I wanted to come play in China," the American said. "I said yes. I felt like it was a great opportunity to make a change and help the team win."
At the time, signing Allen was something of a gamble. Chinese clubs usually preferred bigger overseas players who could dominate with their size. Allen was different: an undersized guard with explosive athleticism and a fearless style shaped by years of experience.
"I played a lot of physical basketball, so it was very simple for me," he said. "It was easy. I play better when it's physical."
He quickly changed perceptions.
During the 2008-09 season, Allen averaged 22.1 points, 6.1 rebounds, 6.1 assists and 3.4 steals per game, leading Xinjiang to the CBA Finals for the first time in its history. The following season, the team reached the championship series again.
One moment from his CBA debut remains especially clear in his memory. Against the Beijing Ducks, Allen hit a game-tying shot to force overtime and eventually helped Xinjiang secure the victory.
"Even our coach, who was always calm, was kind of nervous," Allen recalled. "I told him, 'Don't worry.' I just made the shot. I will never forget that."
For Allen, Xinjiang was never just another stop in his career. It was a place he felt a responsibility to fight for, even when injuries tested him.
"I told the coach, 'If I'm not broken, I'm going to play. If I'm not going to hurt the team, I'm going to play.'" he said. "I just wanted to give back to the fans because I feel like there is always someone who probably only gets one chance to see me play. So I wanted to give everything."
BACK TO URUMQI
Allen left Xinjiang after the 2009-10 season, but his connection with the team continued. His WeChat profile picture remains a photograph of him dunking in a Xinjiang jersey, and he tried to attend Xinjiang games whenever the team played near where he was living.
When Xinjiang finally won its first CBA championship in 2017, Allen celebrated the team's success from afar.
"I was happy for the people and the fans because I felt like I let us down," Allen said. "I really felt that way because we didn't win it."
This summer, former teammates invited him back to Xinjiang to work with the club's young players. Some of those former teammates are now members of the team's management or coaching staff.
"Honestly, I wanted to come back years ago to help," Allen said. "I saw some good players and wanted to help them improve, and I was very excited, and this was the perfect time."
Returning to Urumqi after nearly two decades, Allen found a city that had changed significantly. A new airport terminal, modern buildings and expanded roads reflected its development since his playing days.
But some things had not changed. The familiar training facility was still there, and the basketball community welcomed him back warmly.
"I have to say, we're family," Allen said. "They are all my brothers."
He also returned to one of his old traditions: eating dumplings. During his playing days, dumplings were his customary meal before Xinjiang games.
News of Allen's return also excited many fans.
A few days ago, a girl stopped him on a street in the city and showed him a photo on her phone. It was a picture of her father with Allen years earlier. Allen smiled and took a new photo with her to give to her father.
"Those types of things, I cherish them," he said. "All the hard work I put into this game, and 18 years later, they still love me."
"You don't always get that. When your team is doing bad, fans don't always love you. But here, they love you when you're doing good and when things are difficult. That gives you a reason to play hard all the time," he said.
NEW MISSIONS
Unlike many foreign players and coaches who live outside the team facility, Allen chose to stay in the team's dormitory.
His reason was simple: he wanted to devote all his time to helping Xinjiang's young players improve.
"I don't want to waste time commuting or doing other things," he said. "I just want to focus on helping the young players improve."
Every night, Allen stays after practice to work with four or five young guards, helping them prepare for the new season. He often joins team training sessions himself, competing alongside the players. That has led some fans to joke that Xinjiang should sign him again as a player.
"It's crazy," he said. "I thought about it because I still play basketball with young guys, I train all the time. I'm still doing everything except dunking."
After Xinjiang endured a disappointing season, Allen hopes to help rebuild the team's winning culture.
"Xinjiang is a winning team," he said. "It's not a losing team."
During his playing career, Allen was known for embracing Xinjiang's demanding training culture. Unlike some overseas players who struggled with strict coaching methods, he enjoyed the intense competition.
"We practiced hard and always played hard against each other," Allen said. "I loved that because if we played hard in practice, it made us better in games."
He wants young players to understand that basketball is about more than scoring.
"As a point guard, you have to contribute. You have to get your teammates involved, make everybody happy, and then you can score."
The jersey is gone, but the commitment remains.
"I hope people remember that I gave everything I had on the court, and now I'm giving everything I have as a coach," Allen said. ■

US waging ‘genocide without bombs’ against Cuba – South African cleric
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
13:10:47 UTC

US waging ‘genocide without bombs’ against Cuba – South African cleric
South African Anglican priest and anti-apartheid activist Michael Lapsley has accused the US of inflicting “a genocide without bombs” on Cuba through sanctions that he says are causing severe shortages and worsening the island’s humanitarian crisis.
Lapsley made the allegation after returning from Havana, where he said he observed dire conditions and few vehicles on the roads because of severe fuel shortages. He said Cubans endure prolonged electricity outages that prevent water from being pumped, disrupt factories and hamper the production of medicines.
”The United States is actively strangling Cuba. This is a collective punishment of a whole country since the triumph of the revolution. However, things have become immeasurably worse in the last six months,” he told IOL.
Washington has maintained an embargo on Cuba since 1962.
In January, US President Donald Trump declared a national emergency over Cuba and moved to restrict its fuel supplies, blocking oil tankers bound for the island and threatening tariffs against countries that continued supplying it. Cuban Energy and Mines Minister Vicente de la O Levy said in May that the country had run out of diesel and fuel oil, leaving it dependent on gas from its own wells. Island-wide blackouts have been reported since March.
Lapsley travelled to Havana earlier this month to attend a colloquium marking the centenary of the birth of Fidel Castro, who led the 1959 Cuban Revolution and ruled the island for almost half a century. Castro died in 2016.
Delegates from 63 countries attended the event, including representatives of South Africa’s National Education, Health and Allied Workers’ Union (Nehawu), the South African Communist Party (SACP) and former minister Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma.
During an address to the gathering, Lapsley called for an end to the US blockade of Cuba. Joel Ortega Dopico, president of the Cuban Council of Churches and the Cuban Bible Society, told Lapsley that Washington’s restrictions were making it difficult even for countries seeking to assist Cuba.
“They don’t allow diesel or oil to get into the country. It’s very difficult. Support from other countries, even from countries that want to support Cuba, is very hard. They are making it hard for everyone to help Cuba right now,” Dopico said, adding that the restrictions were hitting the most vulnerable hardest, with some Cuban families cutting their food intake from three meals a day to one.
“Access to basic foods like eggs, milk and rice is very hard in Cuba, because if you don’t have diesel, if you don’t have technology, if you don’t have access to that, you cannot produce,” he said.
Lapsley said Cubans had shown resilience and innovation but now needed international support. “From the beginning, Cuba has fought for other countries, such as South Africa, Angola and Namibia. Now, the world needs to come to their support. Governments, solidarity movements and faith organisations need to come together so Cuba can survive. But they also need to come together to oppose what the United States is doing,” he stressed.
Lapsley is honorary life president of the Friends of Cuba Society, which he helped establish ahead of South Africa’s first democratic election in 1994. He also brought medical supplies to Cuba during the visit.

Tokyo-bound express train hits and kills four workers at railway station in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-20
13:10:27 UTC
22:10:27 KST

Railway officials said it was unclear why the workers did not leave the site when the train was approaching, or what the lookout people were doing.
Four people doing weed control work on a railway track in Japan were killed after being hit by an express train as it entered a station where they were working, officials said on Thursday.
The accident occurred at Shin-Kanuma Station, north of Tokyo, and involved the Tokyo-bound Spacia express train, the Tochigi prefectural police said.
The four, three workers and a supervisor, were rushed to a hospital but later pronounced dead, according to police and train operator Tobu Railway Co.
Six other people at the site, two other workers, three on lookout duty and an on-site supervisor, were safe, Tobu Railway said.
They had been assigned to spray herbicide. About 50 passengers on the train were also uninjured.
Railway officials said it was unclear why the workers did not leave the site when the train was approaching, or what the lookout people were doing. They said they are cooperating with authorities investigating the cause of the accident.
Those on lookout duty are supposed to warn fellow workers of an approaching train by waving a flag, using a whistle or a microphone.
Takao Suzuki, head of Tobu's railway business division, apologised for the fatal accident. “We take this severe accident seriously and we will ensure preventive measures and never let this happen," he said.
Trains on the line were suspended for several hours, but services resumed later on Thursday, officials said.
Fatal train accidents are rare in Japan, which has a reputation for safe and punctual transportation.

The videos spread disinformation about Swedish politicians’ alleged ties to paedophiles and financial criminals, claims of planned election fraud, and attacks on opposition leaders. Alongside Swedish politicians, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has also been targeted. The information was shared with The Insider by the Antibot4Navalny project.
One video uses Der Spiegel branding to claim that the Greek government froze the financial operations of more than 500 companies linked to Merz and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. The entities were allegedly involved in laundering proceeds from drug trafficking and financed a paedophile network known as “04/09.” This likely refers to Operation Fever, a Polish police initiative that saw a network of more than a hundred criminals arrested across 12 countries on April 9, 2025. Matryoshka’s video also invokes the former head of Poland’s Military Counterintelligence Service, Radosław Kujawa, who allegedly described the events as “a victory for the Swedish and German opposition.”
Another video, circulated with the caption “Sweden’s ruling coalition uses the same tactics against its political opponents as Germany’s CDU party,” uses the logo of Swedish broadcaster SVT. The video claims that Landa, a lobbying organization linked to the CDU, was spreading disinformation to discredit Swedish opposition figures.
Another clip, which mimics Euronews content, claims that German hackers broke into Sweden’s BankID identification system to influence the elections.
Sweden’s Riksdag elections are scheduled for Sept. 13. The elected members of parliament will then choose a new prime minister. The ruling coalition — comprising the Moderate Party, the Christian Democrats, the Liberals, and the Sweden Democrats — faces a left-wing coalition of Social Democrats, the Left Party, the Greens, and the Centre Party. Polls show the left-wing coalition leading by around 10 percentage points (53.9% to 43.9%), making a change of government highly likely.
Several regional and local elections in Germany are also taking place in September. As The Insider reported earlier, Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) issued an official warning about a Russian-led disinformation campaign. According to the agency, this month Matryoshka bots spread posts on X using the hashtag #TimeToDivideGermany, promoting the idea of re-dividing Germany into East and West while calling such a division a “historical necessity.”

Gaza holds mass funeral for 50 Palestinians killed in Israeli genocidal war
The funeral procession took place weeks after the bodies of 112 Palestinians were buried in another mass funeral, having been recovered from the site of a November 2023 Israeli attack in Sabra.
At least 50 Palestinians whose bodies were retrieved recently from the rubble have been laid to rest in Gaza City, in the latest mass funeral held in the enclave for victims of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
The funeral ceremony on Thursday came weeks after search and rescue teams recovered the bodies from the site of Israeli air strikes in the early months of the war, which began in October 2023, from the neighbourhoods of Tal al-Hawa, Zeitoun, Sabra, Sheikh Radwan and Shati, Al Jazeera correspondent Ghazi al-Aloul reported.
